newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Confusion on Zaire refugee numbers as planners meet.
newsitem.headline: Confusion on Zaire refugee numbers as planners meet.

text.p: Complete confusion about the number and location of Hutu refugees and homeless Zaireans wandering in eastern Zaire reigned on Friday as planners for a stalled military intervention force met in Germany.
Despite confident and neat numbers from the U.N. refugee agency (UNHCR) in Geneva, pinpointing the 700,000 refugees, the reality on the ground was chaotic.
Neither displaced Zaireans, rebels, refugees nor other U.N. agencies could confirm what the UNHCR has stated based on satellite photographs and overflights.
The confusion complicated the task of representatives from about 40 countries and aid organisations meeting at Kelly Barracks at the U.S. army base in Stuttgart, southwest Germany.
The experts, relying on satellite imagery and other data, will assess options to get assistance to the refugees and whether an approved U.N.-backed military force is needed.
Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said on Thursday the meeting would not decide whether to send a force.
"There will not be a decision in Stuttgart. It is a meeting to look at all the factors and all the options, and after that there will be a context for a decision," he said.

An estimated 500,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees have returned home from eastern Zaire over the past week to escape fighting between Rwandan Hutu extremists, the Zairean army and Zairean rebels in the area.

Aid agencies reckon another 700,000 refugees remain, plus at least 250,000 internally displaced Zaireans. Their physical condition after more than a month on the move with scant food, water and medicines, is unknown.
On Thursday, the UNHCR, citing satellite photos as evidence, spoke of a group of 200,000 moving north from Bukavu.

But it also said it had located 250,000 south of Bukavu, as well as 50,000 west of the Masisi region west of Goma, about 100,000 north of Sake in the Masisi plus, deeper into Zaire, and another 100,000 people in the Fizi area, some 100 km (60 miles) south of Uvira.

Yet on Friday in neighbouring Rwanda, the head of a U.S. military assessment team told a news conference he could only be certain of one group of 150,000 to 175,000 refugees heading north from Bukavu.

Major-General Edward Smith said they seemed to be bona fide refugees, not former Rwandan army soldiers or Interahamwe militias. The group was between 100 and 150 km (60 and 100 miles) from Goma, but he could not say if it was heading for Goma, then on home to Rwanda, or would turn northwest away from the border.
Bukavu is about 150 km (100 miles) from Goma by road so it would appear from Smith's statement that some of these refugees would be very close to Bukavu.
U.S. military satellite pictures are known to form part of the basis for all numerical estimates and yet Smith could not confirm the UNHCR assertions.
"I can't speak for the U.N., but I'm confident that with the data we have and the means of getting the figures that we have an accurate estimate," he said.
The U.S. has scaled down its commitment to the Canadian-led intervention force since the 500,000 returned home and is not now planning to contribute combat troops.
The Zairean rebels, backed by Rwanda, declared the refugee crisis was over and there was no need for any foreign force.
They said satellite pictures of people on the move were either refugees closely linked with Hutu militias and former Rwandan army soldiers or internally displaced Zaireans.
"We don't see any need for a military intervention force to come to Zaire, all the refugees have gone to Rwanda, the refugee crisis is resolved," rebel commander Andre Kassesse told reporters.

Kassesse said fighters of the hardline Interahamwe militia and soldiers from the defeated Hutu army, accused of leading the 1994 Rwandan genocide, had taken to the Masisi hills west of Goma, but he said no heavy fighting was currently under way.
"There are only small actions, do the international community want to come and help the Interahamwe?," he asked.
Ray Wilkinson of the UNHCR said on Thursday that UNHCR had reports of heavy fighting in Zaire, south of Minova on Lake Kivu, 20 km (12 miles) south of Sake.
"This appears to confirm the reports we've had for the past four days of a large movement of refugees and Interahamwe from south Kivu towards Sake and the north," he told reporters.
